text: Good evening. I'm Helen Zhou. I'm a family doctor on Fifth Street, and I chair the board at {homeCenter}. $ Since the new federal rules, three of my patients have stopped coming to their follow-ups. One is diabetic. Nobody told them to stay home; they heard the speeches and did the arithmetic. These policies are built to divide a town into the people who get asked for papers and the people who don't, and a divided town is a sicker town. $ [neutral] I'm not here to ask for something for us alone. I'm asking the next governor to keep the clinic, the library and our hall open to everyone, in the languages people actually speak, so nobody has to choose between a checkup and feeling safe.

You asked what I'd want the governor to do first. Two things. Put interpreters at every state-funded clinic desk, and tell every resident in writing that a clinic is not an immigration office. $ And fund the places where people meet each other. This spring our seniors and the library's volunteers ran a health fair together: blood pressure at my table, benefits at the next one. Half the people who came had never been inside the library. $ [warm] I watch young people in this room move between two languages without thinking about it. That isn't a problem to be managed. It's the best thing this town has. Build on it, and don't let Washington teach us to be afraid of each other.

Good evening. I'm Helen Zhou, a family doctor, and I chair the board at {homeCenter}. $ I'll admit I'm in a good mood. This spring the clinic put up a sign: you have the right to an interpreter at no cost. Thirty years of asking, and now it's the rule. That's progress, and I'm not embarrassed to say so. A country that says out loud that everyone belongs in the waiting room is a better country. $ [neutral] But a rule on a wall is only a sign. Somebody has to tell Mrs. Wu she can ask, and walk in with her the first time. That's the work the next governor can help us do, with the library, the schools and every hall like ours.

You asked what the state should do with the money coming from Washington. Spend it where people already cross paths. A citizenship class that meets half at the library and half at our hall. School forms in more than one language, with a person to explain them. $ And invite everyone. At our autumn festival I want the mail carrier, the librarian and the family who moved in last month at the same table, arguing about the mooncakes. $ I see young people here who switch languages mid-sentence and never notice. They're the bridge we keep talking about. Give them a reason to stay, and work worth doing on both sides of Grand.
That's exactly it: both doors open, and you walking through them. Come find me after. I have a sign-in table that needs someone with two languages.
I hear you, and English matters; I tell my patients the same thing. But nobody should have to stop being who they are to be served at a clinic desk.
I understand wanting to look after our own; half my board says it every month. But the people who need us most are exactly the ones a closed door keeps out.
Listening is a good start. When you're ready to decide, come to the forum at the library. And bring someone who's never been.
Thank you, {playerName}. Whatever you decide, I hope you'll keep showing up in both places.
